The deflection angle of a ray with closest transverse distance \(r_E\) from the lens is \(\alpha=4GM/(c^2r_E)\). Let observer-lens distance be \(D_L\), observer-source distance \(D_S>D_L\), and apparent angular Einstein radius be \(\theta_E\). statement.text:
Gravitational lensing
A point source, a lens of mass \(M\), and an observer are nearly aligned. The deflection angle of a ray with closest transverse distance \(r_E\) from the lens is \(\alpha=4GM/(c^2r_E)\). Let observer-lens distance be \(D_L\), observer-source distance \(D_S>D_L\), and apparent angular Einstein radius be \(\theta_E\). Use \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{SI}\) and \(c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\).
a. Aligned lens geometry
Draw the ideal observer-lens-point-source layout. Show a deflected ray, its deflection angle, Einstein radius, apparent angular radius and measurable distances.
b. Perfect alignment image
Sketch the observed image for exact alignment.
c. Misalignment image
Sketch the image and source-lens geometry when the three bodies are not aligned.
d.escape. Newtonian escape speed
Derive escape speed from distance \(r\) from point mass \(M\).
d.radius. Schwarzschild radius
Set that escape speed equal to c to derive the Schwarzschild-radius expression. Explain the scope of this argument.
e. Radius from deflection
In the aligned case, find \(r_S\) from measured \(\alpha,r_E\).
f. Angular approximation choice
For a lens of a few solar masses at a distance of a few \(10^{18}\,\mathrm m\), and a source a few times farther away, choose independently for \(\alpha\) and \(\theta_E\): large and requiring exact trigonometry, small and permitting small-angle approximations, or irrelevant.
g. Radius from measurable distances
Use the preceding approximation to express \(r_S\) in terms of \(\theta_E,D_S,D_L\).
h. Einstein angular radius
A lens of \(6.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), at \(2.6\times10^{18}\,\mathrm m\), passes in front of a star at \(9.2\times10^{18}\,\mathrm m\). Find the Einstein angular radius at exact alignment.

children.text: Place observer, lens and source on an axis, with the lens between the others. Draw a ray reaching transverse radius \(r_E\) at the lens plane, then bending towards the observer. Label \(\theta_E\) at the observer, total bend \(\alpha\) at the lens, distances \(D_L,D_S,D_S-D_L\). The source-side angle is \(\alpha-\theta_E\). Rotational symmetry creates equivalent rays at all azimuths.

nodes.alt: Original aligned gravitational lens ray diagram, apparent source and observer-source and observer-lens distances.

children.text: Rotational symmetry turns a point image into a circular Einstein ring, centred on the projected lens position, with angular radius \(\theta_E\). A finite-size source broadens the ring.

For an ideal point source and point lens there are two images, on opposite sides of the lens along the line to the unlensed source. For a small-angle source offset \(\beta\), the lens equation is \(\beta=\theta-\theta_E^2/\theta\), with roots \(\theta_\pm=[\beta\pm\sqrt{\beta^2+4\theta_E^2}]/2\). A resolved extended source produces distorted arcs, rather than a complete ring. Show the two rays in the plane containing observer, lens and source. The official marking notes favour arcs and discuss incomplete rings. Those describe an extended or resolved source. For the ideal point-source, point-lens model, the two-image lens-equation result above is the consistent limit. Compare the geometry as well as the sketch.
Zero asymptotic kinetic energy requires \(mv_{esc}^2/2-GMm/r=0\), so \(v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}\).

The substitution gives \(r_S=2GM/c^2\), the same radius as in general relativity. The Newtonian argument reproduces the expression but does not derive an event horizon or the behaviour of light inside it.
Both angles are very small. Small-angle approximations for sine and tangent are valid for both. Neither angle is irrelevant to the geometry.

solution.text:
Gravitational lensing
a. Aligned lens geometry
Place observer, lens and source on an axis, with the lens between the others. Draw a ray reaching transverse radius \(r_E\) at the lens plane, then bending towards the observer. Label \(\theta_E\) at the observer, total bend \(\alpha\) at the lens, distances \(D_L,D_S,D_S-D_L\). The source-side angle is \(\alpha-\theta_E\). Rotational symmetry creates equivalent rays at all azimuths.

b. Perfect alignment image
Rotational symmetry turns a point image into a circular Einstein ring, centred on the projected lens position, with angular radius \(\theta_E\). A finite-size source broadens the ring.
c. Misalignment image
For an ideal point source and point lens there are two images, on opposite sides of the lens along the line to the unlensed source. For a small-angle source offset \(\beta\), the lens equation is \(\beta=\theta-\theta_E^2/\theta\), with roots \(\theta_\pm=[\beta\pm\sqrt{\beta^2+4\theta_E^2}]/2\). A resolved extended source produces distorted arcs, rather than a complete ring. Show the two rays in the plane containing observer, lens and source. The official marking notes favour arcs and discuss incomplete rings. Those describe an extended or resolved source. For the ideal point-source, point-lens model, the two-image lens-equation result above is the consistent limit. Compare the geometry as well as the sketch.
d.escape. Newtonian escape speed
Zero asymptotic kinetic energy requires \(mv_{esc}^2/2-GMm/r=0\), so \(v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}\).
d.radius. Schwarzschild radius
The substitution gives \(r_S=2GM/c^2\), the same radius as in general relativity. The Newtonian argument reproduces the expression but does not derive an event horizon or the behaviour of light inside it.
e. Radius from deflection
Because \(\alpha=2r_S/r_E\), \(r_S=\alpha r_E/2\).
f. Angular approximation choice
Both angles are very small. Small-angle approximations for sine and tangent are valid for both. Neither angle is irrelevant to the geometry.
g. Radius from measurable distances
\(r_E\simeq D_L\theta_E\), and \(\alpha\simeq\theta_E+r_E/(D_S-D_L)=\theta_ED_S/(D_S-D_L)\). Therefore \[r_S=\frac{\theta_E^2D_LD_S}{2(D_S-D_L)}.\]
h. Einstein angular radius
\[\theta_E=\sqrt{\frac{4GM}{c^2}\frac{D_S-D_L}{D_LD_S}}=7.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad},\] about 0.014 arcseconds.
